rv.q: At 90 minutes it is a meal, not quite filling enough but every morsel delicious.
Eleanor Tindall’s meet cute queer love story is appropriately moving, but comes with a lot of very distracting baggage.
The play's name notwithstanding, Tender is tough-minded to its core – and terrific.

Since she’s actively avoiding a former boyfriend, who seems to be stalking her, this might just be a delusion. When she meets Ivy, who works in a coffee shop and lives with her boyfriend Max, and is constantly providing emotional support for her brother Cas, the two women are drawn to each other.

It’s a breathtaking dramatic experience, fuelled by an almost magical romance, unnerving tension, a creative team on song, and two leads who keep the Bush Theatre audience on tenderhooks almost the entire duration.

There is an awful lot in Tender, perhaps too much. The emotional intensity of the love story is always at risk of being lost amid the surreal body horror. But you will remember and root for Ivy and Ash, flawed as they are.
Tender is 1 hour 30 minutes of stellar acting with a script that leaves you aching for a little more.

Tender by name and tender by nature, it throws the kitchen sink and then some at an increasingly convoluted storyline, including self-harm, possible eating disorders and an apparent addiction to adult entertainment.
I quite like a touch of ambiguity, but I did find Tender a bit confusing.

Powered by two outstanding central performances and guided by assured direction and a script that constantly challenges expectations, Tender is an ambitious and absorbing piece of theatre that is well worth seeing.
Tender is a confident and deeply engaging piece of new writing, elevated by two outstanding performances.

cn.t: This queer romance-thriller earns praise for its ambition and strong performances from Amewudah-Rivers and Kemp-Sayfi, though critics split on whether its tonal shifts and surreal twists cohere into a satisfying whole.
